prompt: By the lesson, what separates application, solution and enterprise architecture?
hint: Four things change between the levels, and seniority is not one of them.

choices.text: Seniority: an enterprise architect outranks the other two
choices.why: The lesson says the levels are not ranks, and a decision inside one service can cost more to undo than a roadmap item.

choices.text: Which technologies each level is allowed to choose
choices.why: Technology choices happen at every level; the levels are told apart by scope and horizon, not by a list of permitted tools.

choices.text: Scope, horizon, audience and artefacts
choices.why: Right: how much of the company it covers, how far ahead it looks, who reads it and what gets written.

choices.text: How many diagrams each level produces per quarter
choices.why: Diagram count measures activity, not level; a solution can be designed with one view and a time budget.

prompt: Pricing's floor stage is "the only way out": no quote leaves the service without passing through it. Why does the lesson count that as architecture, even though nobody outside Pricing sees it?
hint: Lesson 1's test: what does it cost to change?

choices.text: Because it is drawn on the company-wide diagram of services
choices.why: It is not on any company diagram; the lesson stresses that none of Pricing's internal choices are.

choices.text: Undoing it would stop guaranteeing quotes respect the ANTT floor
choices.why: Right: a small diff would remove a property the rest of the code relies on, which is what makes the change expensive.

choices.text: Because Renata approved it in a design review
choices.why: Who approved a choice does not make it architectural; its cost of change does.

choices.text: Because the ANTT floor is a legal rule, and legal rules are architecture by definition
choices.why: Regulation is part of the environment, but plenty of legal details are ordinary code. What counts is how costly the structure is to change.

prompt: At Carreto, who makes application architecture decisions for a service?
hint: Lesson 3's advice process.

choices.text: Renata, as the company's architect
choices.why: Renata reviews when asked and watches for leaks; she does not take the internal decisions of seven teams.

choices.text: Tomás, because the CTO answers for technical choices
choices.why: The CTO answers for the organisation; deciding inside each service from there would make him the bottleneck.

choices.text: A review board that meets monthly
choices.why: Carreto has no such board, and a month's wait for internal choices is the gatekeeper lesson 17 warns about.

choices.text: The team that builds it, after asking whoever is affected
choices.why: Right: the people who will live with the decision take it, having sought advice.

prompt: Matching wanted to cache Pricing's quotes for an hour. Why did that stop being Matching's internal business?
hint: Think about what happens at nine in the morning on the day ANTT publishes a new table.

choices.text: It could break a guarantee owned by Pricing
choices.why: Right: stale quotes could fall below a new floor, a rule that belongs to Pricing and to the contract between the two.

choices.text: Carreto's standards forbid caching another service's answers
choices.why: No such standard appears; the fix kept the cache and bounded it with a validity time.

choices.text: The cache would have made Matching slower
choices.why: It would have made Matching faster; speed was the reason for it.

choices.text: Kátia asked Renata to take the decision
choices.why: The lesson has Renata asking a question during a review, not taking over Matching's decision.

prompt: Which of these are application architecture decisions for the Pricing service? Choose all that apply.
hint: Does the choice stay inside one deployable system?

choices.text: Putting the routing provider behind an adapter
choices.why: Yes: an internal structure that decides what changing provider costs, invisible outside the service.

choices.text: Which cloud provider the seven teams share
choices.why: That is shared by every team, which makes it enterprise architecture.

choices.text: Loading the ANTT table as data rather than code
choices.why: Yes: it shapes how Pricing changes when the agency publishes, and stays inside the service.

choices.text: How Payments learns that a delivery was proved
choices.why: That joins Tracking and Payments, so it is a solution decision.

prompt: The Driver team wants to change the format of the GPS positions the app sends to Tracking. Only the Driver team would write code. Where does the lesson's three-question test place it?
hint: The second question asks what other systems rely on.

choices.text: Application, because one team does the work
choices.why: Who writes the code is not the test; the first question fails as soon as another system depends on the format.

choices.text: Enterprise, because the app is installed by thousands of drivers
choices.why: Many users do not make a decision company-wide; it changes no shared platform or standard.

choices.text: Solution, since another system depends on it
choices.why: Right: it changes a contract between two systems, even if one team types the change.

choices.text: Not architecture: a data format is an implementation detail
choices.why: A format another team parses is a contract, and contracts are among the most expensive things to change.

prompt: What is the subject of solution architecture, in the lesson's words?
hint: The boxes already existed at Carreto.

choices.text: The module structure inside each service
choices.why: That is application architecture, owned by the teams.

choices.text: The arrows: who tells whom what, in which order and within what time
choices.why: Right: one outcome across several systems, designed at the boundaries.

choices.text: The portfolio of systems over five years
choices.why: That is the enterprise level's question.

choices.text: Choosing a framework such as TOGAF for each project
choices.why: Frameworks belong to enterprise practice in large companies, and the lesson borrows only their vocabulary.

prompt: In the 24-hour payout budget, proof takes up to 4 hours and the payout up to 1 hour. If Sílvio agreed to shorten the shipper's contest window from 12 to 8 hours, how many hours of slack would be left?
hint: 24 minus the sum of the three steps.

prompt: Why could Payments not learn about proved deliveries from a batch that runs every six hours?
hint: Compare the interval with the slack.

choices.text: Pix rules forbid paying drivers in batches
choices.why: No such rule is in the lesson; the problem is time, measured against the budget.

choices.text: Tracking deletes the proof four hours after delivery
choices.why: Tracking keeps the proof; four hours is how late the proof may arrive.

choices.text: One missed run would use six of the seven hours of slack
choices.why: Right: the budget leaves seven hours for everything abnormal, and a six-hour interval spends almost all of it.

choices.text: The bank partner's API rejects transfers sent together
choices.why: The bank partner's limits are not what rules out the batch.

prompt: Who owns the rule that decides a delivery is proved?
hint: Who already had the photo, the signature and the GPS position?

choices.text: Payments, because it is the team that pays
choices.why: Payments trusts Tracking's word rather than re-implementing the rule.

choices.text: The Shipper app, because the shipper can contest
choices.why: Contesting comes after the proof; the shipper reacts to a decision made elsewhere.

choices.text: Renata, because the rule crosses several teams
choices.why: Renata owns the open questions and the budget; the rule itself sits with the system holding the evidence.

choices.text: Tracking
choices.why: Right: it holds the evidence, so it owns the rule and others rely on it.

prompt: Put the steps of the 24-hour payout in the order they happen after the truck is unloaded.
hint: The contest window starts when the shipper is shown the proof.
items: The Driver app uploads the proof
Tracking marks the delivery as proved
Payments sends the Pix through the bank partner
trap: Paying before the contest window ends is the loss Sílvio refused: money for a load that may not have arrived.

prompt: What was Renata's part in the 24-hour payout?
hint: She built none of it.

choices.text: She wrote the Payments code herself, since it was on the critical path
choices.why: The lesson says she built none of it; an architect on the critical path is a bottleneck lesson 16 warns about.

choices.text: She owned the budget, the contracts and the open questions
choices.why: Right: she held what no single team could, until each question had an answer.

choices.text: She left it to the four teams, as each owned a part
choices.why: Each owned a part and nobody owned the promise; leaving it there is the gap the role was created for.

choices.text: She chose the bank partner
choices.why: The bank partner was already part of the picture, and choosing a vendor was not what made her the owner.

prompt: Which question is enterprise architecture's?
hint: The top box of the figure in the first section.

choices.text: How does one outcome flow across several teams?
choices.why: That is solution architecture.

choices.text: How does this service behave when a dependency fails?
choices.why: That is asked inside one system, at the application level.

choices.text: Which systems should we have at all?
choices.why: Right: and what they should share, judged years out.

choices.text: Which diagram notation should each project use?
choices.why: Notation is a modelling choice, and a framework's checklist is the ceremony Renata leaves out.

prompt: "Quote a freight" is a ___; "the Pricing service" is a system that provides it.
hint: It is written in business words and outlives the systems under it.

prompt: What did Carreto's first capability map show about the CT-e?
hint: Two rows stopped the meeting.

choices.text: SEFAZ had rejected the layout Carreto was using
choices.why: No rejection is in the lesson; the finding was internal and structural.

choices.text: It was issued from two places, and one team knew of the second
choices.why: Right: a hurried script in Payments, which a layout change would have caught nobody else expecting.

choices.text: The monolith had stopped issuing it
choices.why: The monolith still issues it for most loads.

choices.text: Pricing was issuing it before the quote was accepted
choices.why: Pricing quotes; it issues no fiscal document in the map.

prompt: Match each portfolio verdict to what it means.
hint: Four words, each a different future for a system.

pairs.right: maintain it, change it when needed
move what it does somewhere else

right_distractors: rewrite it from scratch next quarter

prompt: How does Renata use TOGAF at Carreto?
hint: A framework is a checklist for a large organisation.

choices.text: She runs its Architecture Development Method cycle each quarter
choices.why: Following it in full would produce documents faster than anyone at Carreto's size could read.

choices.text: She rejects enterprise architecture as an ivory tower
choices.why: She does the work in small form: a map, a portfolio, shared standards.

choices.text: She replaces it with Zachman's framework
choices.why: Zachman is a classification of documents, and she adopts neither in full.

choices.text: She borrows the vocabulary and leaves out the ceremony
choices.why: Right: capability, portfolio and layers are useful words without the full method.

prompt: Why does the lesson put a single logging format at the enterprise level, when each team could pick a good format of its own?
hint: When does the cost of seven formats show up?

choices.text: Its cost appears across teams, when an incident crosses services
choices.why: Right: each format is fine alone; following a request through three of them is where it hurts.

choices.text: Logging libraries carry expensive licences
choices.why: Licence cost is not the argument the lesson makes.

choices.text: Each team's own format would be wrong for that team
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite: seven formats suit seven teams.

choices.text: TOGAF assigns logging to its technology layer
choices.why: The reason is a cost Renata can point at, not a framework's classification.

prompt: Match each level's question to the artefacts that answer it.
hint: Close to the code, between the teams, across the company.

pairs.left: How do these systems deliver this outcome?
Which systems should we have at all?

prompt: A supermarket chain wants to post its loads straight from its own system into Carreto. Shipper, Pricing and the chain's IT team would all be involved. At which level is the design work?
hint: Count the parties and ask who owns the journey.

choices.text: Application, since the Shipper team would write most of the code
choices.why: Most of the code in one team still leaves contracts with Pricing and with an outside system.

choices.text: Enterprise, because the chain is a large client
choices.why: Client size does not change the scope of the design; no shared platform is being decided.

choices.text: Solution: one outcome across teams and an outside party
choices.why: Right: it is in the lesson's list of Renata's solution work for the quarter.

choices.text: None, because integrating a client is a project-management matter
choices.why: Contracts, failure behaviour and who retries what are design questions, whoever manages the project.

prompt: What would treating the duplicated CT-e issuing as a Payments bug have achieved?
hint: A question answered at the wrong level.

choices.text: A permanent fix, since the script lived in Payments
choices.why: Fixing the script leaves untouched whatever let a second issuer appear unnoticed.

choices.text: One script fixed, and room left for the next
choices.why: Right: the cause was that nobody could see the capability across systems, which is an enterprise question.

choices.text: A company-wide standard for fiscal documents
choices.why: A bug fix in one team produces no standard; that would take the enterprise view.

choices.text: A faster CT-e authorisation by SEFAZ
choices.why: Where the CT-e is issued from does not change how fast the authority answers.

prompt: Which of these decisions belong at the enterprise level? Choose all that apply.
hint: What the company runs, and what every team shares.

choices.text: Every team publishes events on the one message broker
choices.why: Yes: a shared standard across the seven teams.

choices.text: Pricing returns a validity time with each quote
choices.why: That is a contract between Pricing and its callers, a solution-level change.

choices.text: The monolith's SMS sender is marked for retirement
choices.why: Yes: a portfolio verdict about a system the company runs.

choices.text: Payout steps run in the order of the time budget
choices.why: That orders one outcome across teams: solution architecture.
